status_summary: Executive Order 14238 (2025-03-14) directed USAGM to be reduced to the minimum its statutes require, and most staff were placed on leave and broadcasting was sharply curtailed. Judge Royce Lamberth (D.D.C.) ruled on 2026-03-07 that Kari Lake lacked lawful authority as acting CEO and on 2026-03-17 vacated the wind-down memo and ordered more than 1,000 employees back to work, but a D.C. Circuit panel stayed that order on 2026-03-31 pending the government's appeal, so employees remained on leave. Leadership has moved toward the State Department: Michael Rigas, Deputy Secretary of State for Management and Resources, was reported named acting CEO around 2026-03-12, and Sarah Rogers, nominated to lead USAGM, had a Senate Foreign Relations hearing on 2026-07-30 at which the committee chair described a possible combined role with the State Department's public diplomacy post. Appropriators agreed in January 2026 to about 653 million dollars for USAGM against a 153 million dollar administration request described as supporting an orderly shutdown (per a Washington Post report syndicated by the Anchorage Daily News), and Congress then enacted FY2026 funding in Division F of Public Law 119-75, signed 2026-02-03; the Congressional Research Service reports 652.70 million dollars for USAGM in that law. Inference: with funding enacted and no disestablishment found, the agency has not been wound down.

timeline.event: President signs Executive Order 14238 (published in the Federal Register 2025-03-20, document 2025-04868), which in Sec. 2(a)(ii) names USAGM among seven entities whose non-statutory components and functions are to be eliminated to the maximum extent consistent with law and whose statutory functions and personnel are to be reduced to the minimum presence and function required by law; Sec. 2(b) requires a compliance report to OMB within 7 days. USAGM announces compliance on 2025-03-15, placing most affected staff on paid administrative leave.

Judge Lamberth issues a preliminary injunction in Abramowitz v. Lake (D.D.C. 1:25-cv-00887, with companion Widakuswara v. Lake) ordering reinstatement of employees and contractors, restoration of grant funding for Radio Free Asia and Middle East Broadcasting Networks, and resumption of VOA programming; the government appeals.

A D.C. Circuit panel, 2-1, stays the reinstatement and funding parts of the injunction, saying the district court likely lacked jurisdiction over those personnel and funding decisions; the programming requirement stays in effect.
The full D.C. Circuit declines to intervene in the panel's partial stay of the April 2025 injunction, so the staff and service cuts can continue while the appeals proceed.

The D.C. Circuit hears consolidated argument in four appeals of the April 2025 orders (Widakuswara v. Lake No. 25-5144, Abramowitz v. Lake No. 25-5145, Middle East Broadcasting Networks v. United States No. 25-5150, Radio Free Asia v. United States No. 25-5151).

A D.C. Circuit panel (Millett, Pillard, Garcia) in Abramowitz v. Lake (No. 25-5314) denies the government's request to remove the VOA director while it appeals the ruling that his removal was unlawful, reasoning that the director is an inferior officer whose removal requires approval of the International Broadcasting Advisory Board, which lacked a quorum.

The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-75, H.R. 7148) is enacted; its Division F carries USAGM funding that CRS reports as $652.70 million ($643.00 million for International Broadcasting Operations and $9.70 million for capital improvements), 24.7 percent below FY2025 enacted and well above the $153.0 million request.

Judge Lamberth rules that Kari Lake, who has not been Senate confirmed, lacked legal authority under the Appointments Clause and the Vacancies Act for the actions that largely dismantled VOA; Lake says the decision will be appealed.

In a court filing after the 2026-03-07 ruling, Justice Department lawyers say USAGM has no CEO succession plan, that no one is serving as acting CEO until a permanent nominee is sent to the Senate, and that it is unclear what the agency may do under the order; the judge had ordered the government to name an acting CEO and outline a succession plan by that day.

TheWrap reports that President Trump nominated Sarah B. Rogers, Under Secretary of State for Public Diplomacy, to lead USAGM, and that Michael Rigas, Deputy Secretary of State for Management and Resources, was named acting CEO; a State Department spokesperson said Rogers would hold both roles if confirmed.

Judge Lamberth rules the near-total wind-down of USAGM unlawful, vacates a March 2025 memo that kept 68 positions, and orders more than 1,000 employees back to work (full-time staff by March 23) and international broadcasting resumed; the White House says the administration could appeal.

A three-judge D.C. Circuit panel (Henderson, Wilkins, Katsas) stays the 2026-03-17 order while the government's appeal proceeds; more than 1,000 employees remain on administrative leave, and the appeal could take months (AP; no vote count given).

A D.C. Circuit panel including Judge Pillard hears argument in the appeal over the 2025 removal of the VOA director and, per Bloomberg Government and a Law360 preview, appears skeptical that the administration could remove him without the approval of the agency's board; no ruling was reported.

The Senate Foreign Relations Committee holds a nominations hearing for Rogers as USAGM CEO; Chairman Risch describes a possible dual role with the Under Secretary post as a way to align operations and messaging, and Rogers's written statement prioritizes stabilizing and modernizing the agency and restoring local-language and transmission capabilities.
